subject: Culture
title: Sanctuary and Asylum
description: A quick, practical guide to Sanctuary and Asylum.

hook.text: A medieval murderer who reached a church doorknob before the mob caught him was legally untouchable for 40 days.

buildup.text: Church sanctuary dates to Roman temples where fugitives could claim divine protection from secular law.

discovery.text: This tradition shaped modern asylum law. The 1951 Refugee Convention echoes the idea of sacred safe harbor.

twist.text: In 2007 an American church sheltered an undocumented immigrant for a year. The tradition still lives.

climax.text: Sanctuary cities directly descend from medieval churches declaring they answered to God, not the state.

punchline.text: The line between law and mercy is always contested.

quiz.question: How long could a fugitive claim church sanctuary in medieval England?

details.summary: The concept of sanctuary — sacred spaces where fugitives cannot be harmed — exists across cultures from medieval Christian churches to ancient Greek temples to modern embassy asylum.
details.whyItMatters: Sanctuary traditions prove that even the most rigid honor systems create safety valves. They are the historical ancestors of modern asylum and refugee protections.
takeaways: Medieval churches offered sanctuary from legal prosecution
Modern embassy asylum follows ancient sanctuary principles
The right of sanctuary was codified in English law until 1623

faq.question: How did medieval sanctuary work?
faq.answer: A fugitive who reached a church door and grasped the sanctuary ring was under the church's protection. They had 40 days to either stand trial or 'abjure the realm' (leave the country forever). Violating sanctuary by dragging someone from a church was a severe offense against God and the Crown.

faq.question: Does sanctuary still exist legally?
faq.answer: Legal sanctuary in churches ended in England by 1623, but the principle evolved into diplomatic asylum (embassies as inviolable spaces) and refugee asylum (protection for those fleeing persecution). Julian Assange's residence in Ecuador's London embassy followed sanctuary logic.
